11.title: Derive a 120° segment
11.prompt: In a radius 21 cm circle, a chord subtends 120°. Find its minor segment area using π=22/7 and exact sqrt(3).
solution: Drop OM perpendicular to chord AB. It bisects the chord and the 120° angle, so OM=21 cos 60°=21/2 and AM=21 sin 60°=21 sqrt(3)/2.
AB=21 sqrt(3), hence triangle area=(1/2)×AB×OM=441 sqrt(3)/4.

checklist: Compare step 1: Sector area=(120/360)×(22/7)×21²=462 cm².

Compare step 3: AB=21 sqrt(3), hence triangle area=(1/2)×AB×OM=441 sqrt(3)/4.
Compare step 4: Segment=462−441 sqrt(3)/4=(21/4)(88−21 sqrt(3)) cm².

11.title: Identify the boundary first
11.prompt: Explain sector versus segment, minor versus major, and how to obtain their major areas.
solution: A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc. A segment is bounded by a chord and its arc. The central triangle is the difference between the minor sector and minor segment.
A minor central angle θ≤180° has corresponding major angle 360°−θ. Except at a diameter, the major region is larger.
Major sector=disc−minor sector; major segment=disc−minor segment. Do not exchange a sector complement with a segment complement.

11.title: Derive arc length and sector area
11.prompt: Use a full turn to derive arc length and sector area for θ degrees. Include units and the perimeter of a sector.
solution: A full 360° turn has arc length 2πr and disc areaπr². By proportionality, θ degrees gives arc=(θ/360)2πr and sector area=(θ/360)πr².
Arc length has length units; sector area has square units. The perimeter of a sector with 0°<θ<360° is its arc plus the two radii, not just the arc.
These forms use degrees. Do not put a radian measure into the degree formula.

11.title: Subtract the central triangle
11.prompt: Explain how to obtain minor segment area for 60°, 90° and 120° central angles.
solution: Minor segment=minor sector−central triangle. For 60°, the triangle is equilateral and its area is(sqrt(3)/4)r².
For 90°, the two radii are perpendicular, so triangle area=r²/2.
For 120°, drop a perpendicular from the centre to the chord. The half-angle is 60°, giving altitude r/2 and chord r sqrt(3), hence triangle area=(sqrt(3)/4)r².
Use the question’s π and sqrt(3) approximations consistently, and keep intermediate values unrounded until the requested final precision.

12.title: Recall the basic solid formulas
12.prompt: Record curved/total surface areas and volumes for the basic solids used in this chapter, with symbols defined.
solution: Cuboid dimensions a, b, c:surface 2(ab+bc+ca), volume abc. Cube edge a:surface 6 a², volume a³.
Cylinder radius r, height h:curved area 2πrh, closed total 2πrh+2πr², volumeπr²h.

12.title: Count only the requested boundary
12.prompt: Explain how to decide which surfaces to count when solids are joined, hollowed, open or resting on the ground.
solution: Break the shape into basic solids, label radii, vertical heights and slant heights, and identify the requested inner or outer boundary.
Joined contact faces disappear from the exterior. Unequal bases can leave an exposed annulus. An open container has no lid surface.
A scooped cavity contributes its curved wall while replacing the original flat opening; it does not simply make surface area smaller.
A ground-supported model can exclude its bottom, as in the bird-bath example. State the interpretation rather than mechanically adding total surface areas.

12.title: Add capacity, subtract occupied space
12.prompt: Explain volume addition/subtraction, displacement, density and the length adjustments used for combinations.
solution: Non-overlapping joined solids have additive volumes; cavities and obstructions are subtracted from the original solid or capacity. Hidden interface faces affect area but have no volume to subtract.
A hemisphere’s axial height equals its radius. Two hemisphere ends reduce a capsule’s straight cylindrical length by 2 r. Two cone ends reduce it by the sum of their vertical heights.
For a brim-full vessel, a fully submerged object displaces water equal to its own volume. Remaining water=capacity−inserted volume, subject to fitting and full-submersion assumptions.
Mass=density×volume. Use compatible units:1 cm³=1 mL, 1000 cm³=1 L, 1000 g=1 kg, 1 m²=10000 cm² and 1 m³=1000000 cm³.

solution: Radius=l/2. Start from 6 l² for the cube.
Remove the flat circular areaπ(l/2)², then add the curved inner hemisphere 2π(l/2)².
Remaining surface=6 l²+πl²/4=(6+π/4)l² square units. A cavity removes volume but its curved wall is an exposed surface.

12.title: Displaced water counts spheres
